claim: The owner of a car is analysed as a complement partly because owners are involved with possessions.
evidence_summary: Cars can have mechanics and insurers as well as owners. CGEL appeals to subject-determiner status here and to oblique parallels in the subject argument.
finding: Compare relational and object nouns while holding the form of the personal oblique constant. Some of the supporting arguments depend on one another.
inference: Does an owner’s plausible involvement with a car make the owner a lexical argument of car?

evidence.passage: §14.1, p. 442. The owner of a car is analysed as a complement partly because owners are involved with possessions.
evidence.example: A car may have an owner, a mechanic and an insurer. Its having no owner at all is coherent. Sister, in its ordinary kinship use, requires a relation to somebody. The plausibility of association with car does not select ownership from the other relations.
evidence.establishes: Genitive subjecthood and oblique complementation partly support one another across pp. 442 and 472. A test for lexical selection must also control the independent constraints on personal of-phrases at p. 477.
evidence.locator: Structural analyses with a genuine rival
evidence.note: Local source (working note, unpublished draft or local copy); not online.
